#4333. BYD in talks to buy Ineos’ French factory as Grenadier moves to US

The French factory Mercedes built for the tiny Smart city car, and that Jim Ratcliffe turned into the home of his Land Rover Defender tribute, could soon be building BYDs.

BYD confirmed today that it has entered exclusive negotiations to acquire Ineos Automotive’s plant in Hambach, France. If it closes, it would be the Chinese giant’s second passenger car factory in the EU after Hungary, and the first time a Chinese automaker buys an existing car plant in Europe.

The other half of the deal is Ineos packing up. Alongside the announcement, Ineos Automotive said it plans to move Grenadier and Quartermaster production to the US, which it says accounts for about 70% of its sales. It has shortlisted US sites, hasn’t named any, and is aiming to start production there in 2028.

The math is simple. Every Grenadier shipped from France to the US gets hit with a 15% tariff, and the Quartermaster pickup falls under the 25% tariff on imported pickups. When 7 out of 10 of your customers are American, building your trucks in Lorraine stops making sense.

Ineos says it will keep building both models at Hambach “for the medium term” if the sale goes through, so the two companies would share the site for a while.

Neither side disclosed a price or a closing date, and the sale still has to go through consultation with employee representatives. BYD will soon find out that France is nothing like China when it comes to employee representation. There’s also no word yet on which BYD models would come out of Hambach or when. Same for the plant’s roughly 1,000 employees: BYD made no commitment on how many it would keep.

BYD executive vice president Stella Li said the company wants to give European consumers “vehicles built in France” that use BYD’s technology.

Hambach opened in 1997 as “Smartville,” Mercedes’ factory for the Smart Fortwo, and it later built the all-electric Smart EQ Fortwo. Ineos bought it from Mercedes at the end of 2020 after dropping its plan to build a new factory in Wales, and Grenadier production started in 2022. Ineos says it has put nearly €540 million into the site since 2019.

Capacity is about 30,000 Grenadiers a year. That’s not much by BYD’s standards. BYD sold 3,561,615 passenger vehicles globally in the first 10 months of the year, which means 30,000 units is less than three days of its output.

There’s also a bit of irony in who’s buying. Ineos unveiled its first EV, the Fusilier, in early 2024 while romanticizing gas cars at the same event. A few months later, it shelved the electric model indefinitely, blaming “reluctant consumer uptake” of EVs. Now it’s selling its only factory to the world’s largest EV maker.

This isn’t a surprise. Back in May, Stella Li said BYD was in talks with Stellantis and “other companies too” to take over underused plants in Europe, and that BYD would rather own and run a plant than form a joint venture. Hambach fits that description exactly.

BYD’s first European car plant, in Szeged, Hungary, started trial production earlier this year and is expected to reach mass production in early 2027, with the Dolphin Surf and Atto 2 first in line. BYD eventually wants more than 150,000 vehicles a year out of it. Its separate factory project in Turkey has been put on pause.

The motivation is regulatory. China-built BYD EVs face a 17% countervailing duty in the EU on top of the standard 10% car tariff, imported Chinese hybrids are now subject to quotas, and the EU’s proposed “Made in Europe” rules would tie EV subsidies and public contracts to how much of a vehicle is built locally. A French plant solves a lot of those problems at once.

And BYD isn’t alone. Leapmotor started building the B10 at Stellantis’ Zaragoza plant in Spain in October, Dongfeng plans to build cars at a Stellantis factory in France, Geely is reportedly lining up a Ford plant in Spain, and Chery already assembles vehicles in Barcelona.

Chery is the one BYD should watch. Through October, BYD registered 320,445 vehicles in Europe, up 133%, according to Automotive News. Chery Group was just ahead with 320,631, up 235%. A gap of 186 cars.

Europe matters more than ever for BYD because home isn’t going well. BYD brand sales in China fell 40% to 1,544,699 vehicles over the first 10 months, and its global passenger vehicle sales are down 2.7%.

This is a smart, cheap move for BYD. Building Szeged took years, including land disputes with private owners. Hambach comes with a trained workforce, a paint shop, a supplier base on the German border, and a seller that’s motivated to leave. You don’t get a much easier entry into France, but the easiest in France is still probably more difficult than anything BYD faced in China when it comes to deploying new production capacity.

The 30,000-unit capacity is small, but BYD isn’t buying it for what it builds today. It’s buying a “Made in France” label ahead of local content rules.

I'm guessing BYD is gambling on the French not making it too difficult as it would deter future investment. They're probably also going to use a lot of robots.

We also can’t ignore the symmetry here. Ineos is leaving Europe to build in the US because of tariffs. BYD is buying into Europe because of tariffs. That’s protectionism moving factories. Europe keeps the jobs, and the workers who used to build Smart EVs might get to build EVs again.

And yes, it’s funny that BYD is moving into the home of the Grenadier, a vehicle that exists because Ratcliffe loved the old Defender, days after a court in The Hague barred BYD’s Ti7 from the EU for infringing Land Rover’s Defender design.

The real question is what BYD puts on the line in Hambach. If it’s battery-electric cars, great. If it’s plug-in hybrids built to get around quotas, Europe is trading one gas-burning 4×4 factory for another.

#4329. Volvo Is Bringing Humanoid Robots Into Its Factories. Here's When They'll Start Working

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Volvo, the maker of the EX60 electric crossover, wants to replace some factory workers with humanoid robots that are capable of doing repetitive tasks without complaining about back pain.

To make that happen, the car manufacturer has brought in the first Aeon units at its factory in Ghent, Belgium, where humans are currently training them to do various tasks. Volvo said that it aims to support employees in repetitive and “ergonomically challenging work,” and it’s not the only car company that’s leaning towards replacing humans with robots.

Volvo Cars is training AEON humanoid robots for future work in factories

While fixed robotic arms have been a staple of automotive factories for decades, some brands are now investing a lot of time and money in artificial intelligence-powered robots that can do tasks where components don’t always land in the same exact spot. So-called pick-and-place jobs are gradually being taken over by robots, with Tesla, General Motors, Ford, and Rivian slowly but surely filling their factories with complex robots.

Volvo is no different, and while the first humanoids shipped to the company’s plant in Ghent are only being trained right now, they’ll gradually start going to work in real conditions starting in mid 2027, the Swedish manufacturer said.

Currently, Volvo Cars is using imitation learning to teach the robot how to pick up and place certain components into two fixtures with high precision. Through the learning process, the team will gradually make the work more challenging, adding multiple parts, moving around the production area, and interacting with the plant’s automated systems.

“Aeon’s humanoid design means it can fit into our production as it is today, alongside our teams and existing automation,” says Magnus Nilsson, Chief Manufacturing Officer at Volvo Cars. “Our aim is for humanoid robots to take on some of the most physically demanding tasks and help make work more ergonomic for our people.”

The robot chosen by Volvo looks like a human, but it doesn’t have feet. Instead, the 5.4-foot (1.65-meter) robot moves on wheels and is capable of reaching up to 5.3 miles per hour (8.6 kilometers per hour). It weighs 132 pounds (60 kilograms) and can carry up to 22 lbs (10 kg). Several cameras and sensors are used to capture its surroundings and handle parts with precision.

#4328. Battlefield Labs is coming back for a short session to test out next week's Battlefield 6 update, and you can expect more tests in the future, too

Battlefield Labs is evolving, as it reopens its doors for its next - unusual - session.

Battlefield Studios is seemingly trying something different with Battlefield 6’s next patch, which everyone assumed would be a standard, mid-season update not intended to change the game significantly.

However, it appears that it may bring more to the game than we realised, enough that the developer sees it as an excuse to bring back the pre-launch Battlefield Labs testing initiative.

The December 9 patch kicks off the final phase of the game’s first season, which is set to take the game through the holidays and into the new year. We’ve known about its content for a while, and it’s definitely the lightest, compared to the two previous phases.

Battlefield Studios announced a host of new changes that will be included in the same patch, which are apparently significant enough to require player testing. The developer is reviving Battlefield Labs to help it do so, but only for three two-hour sessions, split across the game’s three main server regions (EU, NA, APAC).

All tests are scheduled for today, December 2, and they remain under NDA. Battlefield Labs is also sticking with PC as its chosen platform yet again, though you will be able to join through Steam this time, alongside the EA app.

The focus of the test will be on three key areas that the December 9 patch will be touching. First, there’s footstep audio, an issue that was really brought into focus with the launch of Redsec Battle Royale. You can expect to hear enemy footsteps from farther away, and intuitively know the type of surface they’re moving on.

The patch also brings another pass to hit registration and netcode, which BF Studios says should improve responsiveness in close-quarter situations. Finally, there are broader changes to other combat areas that the announcement didn’t elaborate on.

All testing will take place on Eastwood, and Operation Firestorm, rotating between Conquest, and Escalation.

Going forward, Battlefield Studios said to expect Labs to be open to more players, and for the process itself to be smoother. The developer wants to have faster turnaround times, after all, so that the initiative can test smaller changes and be more responsive to player feedback.

Some of the more involved, future sessions will include experiments with map layout changes and various other non-standard compositions of player and vehicle numbers. Of course, you can also expect new maps and modes to be tested in Labs, similar to how the CTE was used in Battlefield 4’s long life.

#4327. VW will pay EV drivers in Germany up to €720 to plug in at home

Volkswagen is giving EV drivers in Germany a reason to plug in at home, even if they don’t need a charge. VW’s charging subsidiary, Elli, is launching a vehicle-to-grid (V2G) program in December that pays drivers up to €720 in the first year for keeping a compatible EV plugged in.

The bidirectional home charger costs €1,995, including tax and shipping. Installation is extra.

Elli pays a plug-in bonus of €0.24 for each eligible hour the EV is plugged into the Elli BiDi DC charger. Sessions have to last at least three hours, and drivers need 250 plugged-in hours a month – a little over eight hours a day on average – to earn the full €60 monthly bonus. VW estimates the full first-year bonus could cover the electricity for around 15,500 km (9,600 miles) in an ID.3 Neo Trend, assuming electricity costs €0.33 per kWh.

Elli’s “V2G Flow” electricity plan covers the home and the car. Elli expects to offer a separate payment later under its “V2G Return” plan, at €0.40 for each kWh the car sends back to the grid. Drivers use Elli’s app to set when they need the car and how much charge they want by then. The system handles charging and, when available, sends power back to the grid according to that schedule.

The 11 kW DC charger supports 400- and 800-volt EVs, but eligibility depends on the model and which functions VW has enabled. The offer spans Volkswagen, Cupra, Škoda, and Volkswagen Commercial Vehicles; the latter has its own ordering process. Drivers also need a compatible smart meter and must complete Elli’s online site check and obtain an installation quote before they can order the charger.

BMW and E.ON opened orders in Germany for their home V2G package for the iX3 in February. VW is bringing its offer to four brands, and it says around 360,000 of its EVs built on VW Group’s shared electric platform in Germany have the technical groundwork for bidirectional charging. Drivers will still need to check whether their specific EV qualifies.

Elli is working with bidirectional charging company The Mobility House Energy to pool the available battery capacity of participating EVs. It plans to expand V2G to more European markets in 2027 and launch a separate vehicle-to-home (V2H) product that would let households use electricity stored in their EV, including surplus rooftop solar saved for later use.

#4326. Driven: 2028 Porsche 718 Boxster EV Prototype Wags Its Tail Like a Mid-Engine Sports Car

The Boxster’s rear-biased weight distribution, which is unusual for an EV, makes it handle like a sports car should.

There’s still a lot that Porsche won’t divulge about its forthcoming 2028 718 Boxster EV, including horsepower, battery capacity, range, pricing, or even its final, un-camouflaged looks. But after some seat time around the handling course at the Porsche Experience Center Los Angeles, we now know what it feels like at—and a little bit beyond—its cornering limits.

Whether you’re welcoming the Boxster’s EV transition or bemoaning the loss of its internal-combustion engines, particularly the iconic flat-six, we think anyone who drives the next-generation 983 Boxster will agree it’s fantastic. The steering, inherited from the 992.2 911 Carrera GTS, is eager and sharp, and rear-axle steering will also be available. You can feel the Boxster’s rear-biased weight distribution in the way its rear end steps out when lifting off the throttle.

In other words, this new EV feels like a mid-engine Boxster, because that’s where the weight is concentrated. Other than some hypercars, such as the Rimac Nevera, the forthcoming electric Boxster rides atop one of the first EV platforms built around a two-seat sports car. The 800-volt battery pack lives entirely behind the passenger cabin, in the place the engine used to reside, which leads to a 40/60 front/rear weight distribution, similar to the gas-powered Boxster’s 45/55 split. And since there’s no battery under the floor, you sit as low as you would in any other sports car.

See all results for new 2028 Porsche 718 EV for sale near 20147

We drove what will become the top Boxster model when it goes on sale after its formal debut in early 2027, but Porsche wouldn’t confirm what it will be called. S? GTS? These models wear Pirelli P Zero R Elect tires—and for the first time—mount on staggered-diameter wheels just like the latest 911. The tires measure 255/35ZR-20 up front and 305/30ZR-21 in back, which is more meat than even the last 718 Spyder RS. The company isn’t saying how much power this Boxster’s single rear motor will make—all electric Boxsters will be rear-drive only—but they do claim the sprint to 60 mph will require less than 3.0 seconds. After experiencing being pinned to the seat by a few launch-control starts, the new Boxster feels every bit that quick.

Porsche says this will be the quickest, most powerful Boxster with the highest cornering and braking performance, with a center of gravity that’s—no surprise—much lower than before. We can attest to feeling tons of grip, but can we feel the EV’s added weight? As the Boxster slithered through transitions and dove into apexes, we can’t say it felt heavy, although the squealing from its wide tires sounded at times more tortured than those we recall from the just-over-3000-pound gas-powered Boxster. Porsche says the Boxster EV’s curb weight will fall somewhere within that of the 911 lineup, which ranges from the 3350-pound Carrera to the 4000-pound Turbo S Cabriolet. Here’s hoping it’s toward the lower end of that range, which would be very light for an EV.

See all results for new 2028 Porsche 718 EV for sale near 20147

While this new electric version looks like a Boxster and the low seating position feels like a Boxster, with a forward view of a quickly disappearing hood, Porsche wanted to add some more nostalgic tie-ins by way of fabricated engine noises and simulated shifts. The Taycan got a similar E-Shift feature earlier this year, but while the Taycan’s engine noises weren’t modeled after a specific engine, the Boxster’s very much pays homage to its past. The Boxster’s E-Shift, which is controlled by a knob on the steering wheel and can shift automatically or be controlled by steering wheel paddles, mimics the 981 Boxster GTS’s 3.4-liter flat-six, which Porsche engineers say is the high-water mark for flat-six wails. They told us emissions compromises to the most recent flat-sixes made them choose that one from circa 2015. That said, there’s a bit of revisionist history going on with the electric Boxster’s 8000-rpm “redline” versus the actual 7600-rpm redline in its 981 muse. Either way, the noise emanating from the two speakers—one inside the cabin, one outside—absolutely sounds like a flat-six.

Although the synthesized sound is a solid re-creation, we do think it would be easy to identify the real from the facsimile in a blindfolded test. There’s a lot of nuance going on in the sounds of a flat-six belting to redline—intake and exhaust noise, valve and other mechanical clatter—and it’s hard to generate all of that from a couple speakers. That said, after doing a few hot laps with the system on, we believe it adds to the experience, and it felt weird to switch over to silent and shift-free lapping. We think we’d use this more in a sports car like the Boxster than in the four-door Taycan sedan.

What else did we learn? As before, the 983 Boxster has both front and rear trunks, and its NACS charge port, which is hidden behind a powered door in the middle of the rear bumper, is the first from Porsche to accommodate both AC and DC charging. Today’s Cayenne and Taycan electrics have separate ports for AC and DC with the NACS only handling DC charging.

Officially, there won’t be any gas-powered Boxster variants, but who knows what the lifecycle might hold, especially if early sales disappoint. After all, remember when the previous generation went four-cylinder only, but then the flat-six made a reappearance a few years later? While we’re as sad as anyone to see the flat-six and manual transmission leave the Boxster lineup, we think that anyone who drives the new one will agree it’s a great-handling sports car.

#4325. Honkai: Star Rail 3.8 will run for an extra two weeks while Version 4.0 is in the oven

The next Honkai: Star Rail update is upon us, and there's a mix of good - and unusual news.

HoYoverse just hosted a sizeable Honkai: Star Rail Special Program, revealing more than just the game’s next major update. Version 3.8 was the big highlight, of course, with the new release arriving soon, on December 16-17 depending on your server region.

Alongside showing everything coming with this next update, the developer also announced that 3.8 will go on for eight weeks, rather than the usual six. V3.8 is dubbed "Memories are the Prelude to Dreams", and it brings an end to the Amphoreus journey.

The story in "Memories are the Prelude to Dreams" takes place after the final battle of Amphoreus, where Constance "The Dahlia" appears to deliver a twist: the Trailblazer's memories are scattered, with many parts missing.

This final quest revolves around finding them in order to piece together the mystery, and involves a return to Penacony. This memory-hunting adventure is told from the perspective of Firefly, which will also explain how she entered the dreamscape initially and met the squad.

The new playable character is The Dahlia, whose power is linked to the the Remembrance path, which allows her to fabricate memories. Despite taking her powers from the Remembrance, The Dhalia actually follows the Path of Nihility in-game: she’s a 5-Star character who shines in teams dealing Break DMG.

The Dhalia can unleash a Gloomy Zone that causes Toughness Reduction inflicted by allies to trigger Super Break DMG, even before you break your enemies’ Weaknesses. The Dahlia can also invite one teammate to become her Dance Partner, which allows them (and her) to deal additional Super Break DMG each time they attack an enemy. If you trigger her Ultimate after picking a Dance Partner, she applies Type Weaknesses of both partners to enemies.

While The Dahlia is the only new character appearing in this final Amphoreus update, there'll be reruns aplenty, with an unusual third banner phase to make up for the extra long wait for 4.0. Appropriately for her role in the story, Firefly will make her return alongside The Dahlia in Phase 1, while Fugue and Lingsha will both have banner reruns in Phase 2, which is expected on January 7th. A bonus two-week-long Phase 3 will then begin on January 28th, seeing brief reappearances for popular returning characters Aglaea and Sunday, before things (presumably) go back to normal with the new annual update.

Something else to look forward to in 3.8 is The Chrysos Awoo Championship, which invites players to become chimera trainers and compete in team-based battles. The Remnants of Twilight event kicks off with the new patch, too, featuring its own set of challenges. However, HoYoverse have confirmed that there won't be an extra event during Phase 3 — but hopefully that'll give you some time to wrap up the last of the Amphoreus story content, which is longer than the previous four chapters put together.

The 2027 Cadillac Vistiq is available in four trims: Luxury, Sport, Premium Luxury, and Platinum. All are powered by a dual-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) powertrain that delivers a combined 615 hp and 650 lb-ft of torque.

#4323. A Used Cybertruck Is Selling A Month Faster Than A Ford F-150

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

If you had to guess which used pickup found a buyer fastest in October, the Toyota Tacoma would be a sensible bet. It’s America’s best-selling midsize truck and has a reputation for holding its value. Or you might pick the super frugal Ford Maverick Hybrid. But the truck that beat them both was the Tesla Cybertruck.

The data from the new iSeeCars study covers 1.1 million used vehicles that changed hands in October, so this was before Tesla announced it would discontinue the Cybertruck in 2027. The study looked at one- to five-year-old vehicles and ranked models by how long they’d been listed before selling.

The Cybertruck surpassed all other pickups, averaging 39.1 days, compared to 65.5 days for used pickups overall. The Maverick Hybrid came closest at 43.3 days, followed by the Rivian R1T at 45.2 and the F-150 Lightning at 47.4. The Tacoma came in fifth position.

The gap between the two electric pickups at either end of the list was even more striking. A used Chevrolet Silverado EV took 107.5 days to sell, putting it last among the 24 trucks in the study. That’s a 68-day difference between two American electric pickups. Across the wider used market, EVs averaged about 46 days to find a buyer, around nine fewer than hybrids and 15 fewer than gas vehicles.

How quickly a used Cybertruck sold seems to have changed a lot since May 2024, when some sellers were cutting as much as $30,000 from their asking prices after listing their trucks for close to $200,000. By December of that year, we reported that used Cybertrucks were piling up on dealer lots, with data at the time showing they stayed for 75 days, up from 27 in May.

Then owners got a look at what Tesla itself would pay for a used Cybertruck trade-in. One year later, in May 2025, one owner of a $99,990 dual-motor Foundation Series truck got a trade-in estimate of $65,400 after driving it just 6,211 miles.

So even though the Cybertruck was the fastest-selling used pickup in iSeeCars’ new study, it didn’t report what buyers paid, so we don’t know whether owners got their asking price or had to lower it to sell.

Tesla will build the last Cybertrucks at the end of summer 2027, and this will reshape their used market. Elon Musk originally announced production would end around the middle of the year, but then extended the run to fill more orders. And if you order a Cybertruck now, the only one you can get is the $110,000 tri-motor Cyberbeast, so anyone who wants a less expensive dual-motor truck has to look for a used example.

Once the last new Cybertruck is sold, I’d expect collectors and everyday truck buyers to look at used ones differently. Someone after a clean Foundation Series truck with low miles might pay a little extra for one close to home, especially since it could be months before another comes up for sale nearby.

At the same time, someone who just needs an electric pickup to tow a trailer has more options. If a used dual-motor Cybertruck costs about the same as a Ford F-150 Lightning or a Rivian R1T, I suspect that buyer will care more about mileage, condition, and how much battery warranty is left than when Tesla built its last truck.

#4322. New York Bans Post-Purchase Subscriptions on Vehicles

Monthly payments for heated seats? Not in the state of New York.

Are you paying a subscription fee for hardware already installed on your car? Not for much longer, you’re not. At least, not if you live in New York. Governor Kathy Hochul just signed a bill prohibiting automakers, dealers, and other third parties from charging subscription fees for vehicle features that use pre-installed components or hardware. Those heated seats you’re paying for? Get ready to cancel that subscription. That remote start you buy each winter? Treat yourself to an expensive latte from that cafe you like instead.

See all results for used cars for sale near 60007

The new law (S.9348A/A.10411A) doesn’t stop automakers from charging subscriptions entirely, but it does stop them from being able to charge recurring payments for hardware that doesn’t cause them any recurring costs.

Hochul’s office specifically pointed to heated seats, enhanced navigation, hands-free driving, and entertainment options. Heated seats are pretty cut and dry, but hands-free driving poses an interesting question. Systems such as Tesla’s Full Self-Driving (FSD), GM’s Super Cruise, and Ford’s Blue Cruise all require customers to pay for a subscription to operate. All three systems work with the hardware installed on their respective vehicles, but the automakers could—and likely will—argue that they have recurring costs to keep the systems updated and safe.

Car and Driver reached out to Governor Hochul’s office for clarification on how the law will affect hands-free driving systems. We will update this story if we hear back. Meanwhile, the new law will go into effect on February 27, 2027, giving automakers and third-party companies time to enter into compliance.

#4321. This miniature electric Bentley is ridiculously cool – and actually street legal

If you’ve ever looked at a classic 1929 Bentley Blower and thought, “That looks great, but could it be smaller, electric, and somehow still cost six figures?” then good news: your car has arrived.

Hedley Studios has completed the first 25 production Bentley Blower Jnrs, with the hand-built electric mini-cars now heading to customers. Deliveries are beginning in the UK before expanding across Europe.

The Blower Jnr is an officially licensed collaboration with Bentley, recreating the famous 1929 Bentley 4½ Liter Supercharged Team Car No. 2 at 85% scale. Unlike many scaled-down collector cars, though, this isn’t merely an expensive toy for cruising around your estate. It’s actually road legal.

In the UK and EU, the Blower Jnr is homologated as an L7e quadricycle, reaching over 50 mph (80 km/h) and offering a certified 75-mile (120 km) range. A separate US program is also planned, though it’s not clear exactly what classification the mini-EV would receive stateside.

Underneath the delightfully old-school bodywork is a decidedly newer 48V electric drivetrain producing 31 hp (23 kW). The electric motor sits across the rear axle, while batteries and power electronics are packaged underneath the car.

The carbon-fiber tub rides on a steel frame with leaf springs and period-style friction dampers, while Brembo disc brakes handle stopping duties up front.

Every car that people ever loved will come back in some electric version that they can actually drive and love.

There are some particularly fun details, too. The charging port is hidden inside a recreation of the original Bentley’s supercharger housing, while modern necessities like indicators, headlights, and even a reversing camera have been incorporated without ruining the 1929 aesthetic.

The first 25 cars are part of a nearly sold-out run of 99 First Editions. Another 250 configurable cars will follow, bringing total production to just 349 units.

And “Jnr” definitely doesn’t mean junior pricing. Configurable cars start at £112,500 before taxes – roughly $148,000 at current exchange rates.

Then again, if you’re buying a hand-built miniature electric Bentley, value probably wasn’t the first thing on your mind.

#4320. Every Brand Selling Hybrid Vehicles in the U.S. for 2027

Hybrid car sales are at a high, and that means plenty of choices in segments including SUVs, sedans, vans, and sports cars.

For all the talk about electric vehicles over the past several years, the bigger story is the current hybrid wave. From 2024 until the end of September 2026, gas-electric hybrids soared from just over eight percent of new light-duty vehicle sales to 16 percent, or double the share of EVs, according to the Energy Information Administration. After consecutive years of parallel growth that saw battery-electric and gas-electric vehicles rise together starting in 2020, hybrid sales have never been higher while EVs, despite a spurt in 2025 and 2026, are not recovering.

This means that there’s now more choice than ever among hybrid vehicles: nearly every major automaker offers at least one hybrid model, and many of them offer a wide range of hybrids in various body styles from SUVs to sports cars and everything in between. Here’s a guide to all hybrids on sale, across all segments (excluding 48-volt hybrids that are not designed to power a vehicle solely with electric motors).

Every Brand Selling Sports Cars | Every Brand Selling EVs | Best-Looking Cars

Bentley makes the world’s only four-seat plug-in hybrid convertible, the Continental GTC. The ravishing powertrain, standard with 671 horsepower or 771 horsepower in the Speed and Mulliner, isn’t exclusive to the the Continental range, either. The twin-turbo V-8 and its 22-kWh battery pack are shared with the Flying Spur sedan, both of which claim 30 miles of electric range (we did 49 in the Continental). A turbo V-6 and an 18-kWh battery are found in the Bentayga Hybrid SUV.

BMW offers a sextet of plug-in hybrids that throw heavy punches under hard acceleration. The 550e, 750e, and X5 xDrive50e share a 483-hp setup with a turbo inline-six good for between 34 and 44 miles of electric range, while the M5, M5 Touring and XM electrify a twin-turbo V-8 for a total of 717 or 738 horsepower. We expect to see more hybrid setups on the high-performance end of the lineup in the future, although the next-gen M3 is also offering a fully electric variant, signifying a possible shift in BMW’s strategy.

Chevrolet’s sole hybrids are found within the Corvette lineup. The first is the Grand Sport X, which supplements the base Stingray’s 6.7-liter V-8 with a front electric motor for a total of 721 horsepower. The other is the ZR1X, which costs a quarter-million dollars and pumps 1250 horsepower from a turbo 5.5-liter V-8 and a front electric motor. It gets 12 mpg in the city and goes 225 mph. It’s beyond magnificent. Still, Chevy is planning more mainstream hybrids, as the three-row Traverse SUV is poised to get a hybrid variant in the future.

All mid-engine Ferraris come as hybrids—and 869 horsepower is the bare minimum. That’s the output from the twin-turbo flat-plane V-6 and axial-flux motor in the new 296 Speciale. The wedgy 849 Testarossa stuffs a twin-turbo V-8 and triple motors for 1036 horsepower. For $3.7 million, the almighty F80 goes backward in cylinder count (but with a more powerful twin-turbo V-6 and three motors) and forward with F1 tech for 1184 horsepower. Buy a front-engine Ferrari and you’ll have to settle for nonhybrid V-12s and V-8s.

Ford sold some of the industry’s first PHEVs in the 2010s—remember the Fusion Energi?—but no longer offers any hybrid sedans or SUVs. The Escape Hybrid and PHEV are gone. But one of our favorite hybrids on sale is the Maverick compact pickup, which can hit 40-plus mpg in the city with front- or all-wheel drive. The F-150 PowerBoost, which uses a twin-turbo V-6 with an electric motor, is more capable but not as smooth to drive as the Maverick.

The first Genesis hybrids aren’t launching until the 2028 model year in the U.S., but we decided to include them here anyway. The lineup includes the gorgeous G80 mid-size luxury sedan and the stately GV80 mid-size luxury SUV. Their hybrid powertrains both use turbo 2.5-liter inline-fours and represent the next stage of the Hyundai group’s hybrid expertise. The batteries now use liquid instead of air cooling, a seven-speed automatic replaces the six-speed, and the torque output (391 lb-ft) matches the twin-turbo V-6 in the 3.5T trims.

Honda has been into hybrids almost as long as Toyota has (see the 1999 Honda Insight), and the company’s current hybrid powertrain is a gem. With direct drive (no transmission), the two-motor, 2.0-liter inline-four setup is quick, efficient, and downright fun. It’s available on the CR-V, the Civic sedan and hatchback, and the Accord sedan, and it’s the only choice on the Prelude coupe.

While the Elantra Hybrid takes a hiatus until 2028, Hyundai’s next-best mileage champ is the Sonata Hybrid, which can surpass 50 mpg and offers generous rear leg room. Hyundai’s three compact and mid-size SUVs, including a new-gen Tucson, get hybrid versions and all offer all-wheel drive. Unlike many mainstream hybrids, Hyundai employs a six-speed automatic instead of a CVT or direct drive. The Tucson plug-in hybrid is no longer available.

While Jeep axed the plug-in hybrid 4xe trims of the Wrangler and Grand Cherokee, an extended-range series hybrid is coming to the Grand Wagoneer with a whopping 647 horsepower. The hybrid-only Cherokee compact SUV comes with only 210 horsepower but up to an estimated 39 mpg city rating.

Like Hyundai, Kia’s diversity of gas, hybrid, and electric powertrains has paid off in spades in terms of sales. There are eight hybrids total in the Kia lineup, with plug-in hybrids available on the Sorento and Sportage (no longer on the Niro). Every SUV has a hybrid option, and so does the Carnival minivan.

Surprised to see Lamborghini peddling hybrids? The brand’s lineup is now entirely hybrid, actually, starting with the plug-in hybrid Urus SUV which comes in 789-hp SE and 801-hp Performante versions. Those SUVs can do an estimated 35 miles on electricity. The 907-hp Temerario is also a plug-in hybrid, offering a pitiful four miles of electric range. But the only hybrid that revs to 10,000 rpm. Then there’s the 1001-hp Revuelto and 1050-hp Revuelto SV which pair a giant V-12 with three electric motors. What a time to be alive.

Leave it to Lexus to combine big power with efficiency. This was the brand that in 2008 gave us the LS600hL, a hybrid flagship that could match the refinement from 12-cylinder German sedans. Now that we live in an SUV world, the LX700h is the modern equivalent—at up to $143,000, it’s the rare four-passenger hybrid SUV with four-wheel drive and a fully reclining rear seat. The TX500h is the next step down (the PHEV is gone for 2027). The RX and NX each offer three hybrid trims including plug-ins, while the new ES350h is now the sole hybrid sedan.

Lincoln moved away from hybrids only to come running back—and they took a long way home. The brand’s two hybrid SUVs, the compact Corsair and mid-size two-row Nautilus, are plucked straight from China, since Ford hasn’t yet carved out factory space for these models in North America. They enjoy a substantial exterior refresh for 2027, too. Each comes with turbo inline-fours and all-wheel drive, while the Nautilus goes screen crazy with a 48-inch display hugging the bottom of the windshield.

While the CX-50 Hybrid uses a Toyota-based powertrain, the CX-90 Hybrid is all Mazda. It’s a nicely styled three-row plug-in hybrid SUV with an estimated 25 miles of electric range. The two-row CX-70 Hybrid is discontinued, but there’s a CX-5 Hybrid on the horizon, though it may not arrive until 2028.

Want a Le Mans racer as a comfortable supercar? There’s no better choice than a McLaren Artura, which has a howling twin-turbo V-6 that has the party trick of leaving and arriving in complete silence. With 11 miles of estimated electric range, it can go nearly three times as far on a charge than a Lamborghini Temerario can. The combined 690 horsepower and McLaren’s light-as-a-feather chassis are heavenly. Choose the coupe or a spider.

While AMG customers weren’t so enthusiastic about the C63 and its F1-derived four-cylinder plug-in hybrid powertrain, they’re happy plugging into turbo-sixes and turbo V-8s on the higher-end models. Every hybrid AMG is PHEV, whether it’s a sedan, wagon, SUV, convertible, or coupe. The E Performance trims of the SL and GT Coupe make more than 1000 pound-feet of torque.

Mercedes-Benz’s three hybrid models are all plug-in hybrids just like their AMG cousins, only less potent. The S580e is our personal favorite, as we were able to reach 58 miles of all-electric range on the highway, handily beating the factory estimate. The GLE500e also shares the same inline-six and delivers similar range, while the GLC350e has an inline-four. Like the AMGs, the GLE and S-class hybrids support DC fast charging, a rare feature on a PHEV.

Mitsubishi was first to market with a plug-in SUV, and it hasn’t really received due credit. Part of it is the premium price the Outlander PHEV commands and its so-so performance, though it’s updated for 2027 with more power. It also has plenty of features, decent interior quality, and a healthy 45-mile electric range. Along with the regular Outlander, it’s also the only three-row SUV in the compact segment.

As the only series hybrid in the mainstream segment, Nissan has made a big splash with the Rogue Hybrid after more than a decade without any gas-electric powertrain in its lineup. Think of the company’s e-Power hybrid setup like an extended-range EV where the gas engine serves only as a generator for the electric motors, but without the plug or the big battery. We like how it drives—a lot.

Porsche’s conventional hybrid powertrain sits in its most prized product, the 911, where the T-Hybrid installs one or two electric turbos and a small battery on the GTS and Turbo S. The models with the E-Hybrid badge are plug-in hybrids. The Panamera has three PHEV choices, including the Turbo’s V-8 powertrain shared with Bentley for up to 771 horsepower. The Cayenne Hybrid has either a V-6 hybrid setup or a similar V-8 setup in either the SUV or Coupe body style.

#4319. Tomorrow’s Battlefield 6 patch is the first step towards improving footstep audio, and it might actually fix the settings reset bug

The next major Battlefield 6 patch is nearly upon us, and Battlefield Studios is promising a bounty of changes - including a couple of fixes to some big bugs.

Battlefield 6 is about to receive a new update. Version 1.1.3.0 is set to arrive tomorrow, December 9 to kick off the third and final phase of the game’s first season. Winter Offensive brings some holiday-themed new content to the game, but it’s not the most interesting part of the patch.

That honour goes to a couple of the high-level changes Battlefield Studios has included with the new patch, which range from a major pass on audio to a fix for a particularly annoying bug that’s been seemingly introduced with a recent patch.

Thew new content takes the form of a limited-time version of the game’s Empire State map, which covers it in snow and tweaks its layout slightly. To go along with that there are new limited-time modes for both multiplayer and Redsec’s Gauntlet. The event mode will be available in Conquest, and Domination.

The Ice Climbing Axe is the only new weapon in this drop. The battle pass gets a new Winter Offensive bonus path, just like we’ve seen with previous seasonal stages. This is how you unlock the axe, too.

Easily the most interesting change in this update is the range of improvements to audio across the board. First, footstep audio received a big pass that should make it easier to hear enemy footsteps, easier to locate them, and across different surfaces.

Some of the bugs that caused certain sounds to simply vanish have been fixed. This was especially prevalent in battle royale matches. BF Studios explained in the patch notes that it has adjusted memory priorities for in-game sounds in order to prioritise the most crucial ones. This is not the end of the road on audio, however, as the developer continues to work on making the soundscape more stable and reliable.

Some of those audio changes are the result of recent testing done in Battlefield Labs, which is also responsible for another exciting addition in this latest patch: improvements to hit registration.

While BF6 has had solid and stable netcode, certain situations would sometimes create uncertainty about how you died, and why certain actions seemingly failed to perform at that particular moment.

The focus in this update is to improve the reliability of how actions in close-quarter combat are translated, which includes firing before fully going into ADS, quick aim changes and more.

Speaking of close-range, the patch also brings another pass to soldier visibility to make it easier for enemies to stand out from the background. This is particularly relevant in areas with low contrast, or busy environments with lots of particle and visual effects.

1.1.3.0 also brings yet another set of weapon handling and gunplay tweaks, this time focusing on accuracy issues with first shots. You can also expect more tweaks to attachment behaviour with regards to recoil.

Something else worth highlighting is that vehicle gameplay is getting several smaller tweaks that have to do with how they interact with the world, how their HUDs behave and more. Finally, your settings should no longer be reset after applying an update. BF Studios says there are still some instances where that might happen, but the issue should be fixed for the majority of players.

You can read the full change log on the Battlefield blog.

#4317. Narrowed Focus: 1997 Toyota Camry LE Tested

One of America’s favorite family haulers gets a full makeover.

Over 3,000,000 sold! Call it the McCamry. Along with the Ford Taurus and the Honda Accord, this Toyota is right at the top of the list when Amer­ican families go new-car shopping, and right at the top of the ratings in our last family-sedan comparison test (November 1995). Since its introduction here in 1983, Toyota has diligently smoothed up, slicked up, and suaved up the Camry till the only remaining awkwardness is the unlikely spelling of its name.

That won’t change as Toyota introduces its fourth-­generation Camry in Sep­tember, and neither will the mix of virtues that make this model a favorite. We’re talking refinement of the Camry theme, not reinvention. In fact, the basic platform and powertrain carry on, though engineering improvements seem to touch every part of the car. It’s slightly bigger in each exterior dimension—0.7 inch longer, 0.4 inch wider, 2.1 inches longer in wheelbase; the same four­-cylinder and V-6 engines are modestly more powerful (up 8 hp in the four, up 6 hp in the V-6); and the interior has been upgraded to meet all the safety standards scheduled in the next few years, including the 1997 side-impact and 1999 head-­impact requirements. The aerodynamic drag coefficient has been improved to 0.30, from 0.33.

See all results for used 1997 Toyota Camry for sale near 50317

Toyota is, however, tightening the Camry’s focus. It’s available only as a four-door now in three trim levels: CE, LE, and XLE. Gone is the coupe, which won over just five percent of Camry buyers. Gone, too, is the station wagon, a shape that convinced only three per­cent of Camry buyers in its losing battle against the tide of minivans. (Production of a Camry-based minivan begins next spring.)

In the past, we’ve joked that the Camry’s personality is one of aggressive bland­ness. Unlike the frisky feeling of the Accord and the athletic tautness of the Dodge Intrepid, both of which come through loud and clear before you’ve driven to the first corner, the Camry’s subtlety grows on you over time. It’s smoother, softer, quieter than the others, less com­municative, less mechanical. Instead of talking to you in the very pleasant way of those others, it’s the silent type that, you soon notice, goes expertly about its job.

In this new Camry, Toyota sharpened the expertise without changing the per­sonality. It’s still a car that’s light to the touch: easy to steer, easy to brake. The ride is commendably free of harshness, thanks in part to mounting the suspension on isolated crossmembers front and rear. The four­-cylinder version, with its 195/70SR-14 tires, rides very smoothly and ignores almost completely the road textures that create so much droning in sporting cars. The V-6s come with 205/65HR-15s on six­-inch-wide wheels. These tires are noticeably harsher and noisier than those on the four-cylinder cars, though road nose is still quite reasonable when compared with other cars in this class. Road grip and handling predictability are well above the minimums we’d set for family cars.

See all results for used 1997 Toyota Camry for sale near 50317

The Camry V-6 has been one of the top performers in this class. The 1997 model gains six horsepower (now 194 hp at the same 5200 rpm as the previous peak), gets shorter final-drive gearing (3.93 versus 3.43), and weighs about the same as last year’s smaller car. Another performance plus: A manual transmission has returned to the V-6 lineup, available only on CE models. How­ever, our LE V-6 auto­matic was no quicker than the last LE V-6 we tested, managing 0 to 60 mph in 8.3 seconds. Expect the five-speed to trim that by about four-tenths.

On the road, the automatic’s eagerness to change down a gear or two when you press the pedal, even slightly, and the seamless smoothness of those changes give this car quick reflexes in traffic. The engine revs with the hushed moan of a Lexus. This year, traction control is optional on LE and XLE V-6 models. When it comes to powertrain pleasures, the Camry is world-class.

Still, it’s the more subtle details of pas­senger accommodation that make this Toyota a family favorite. In the previous­-generation Camry, our comparison tests show two adults fit in the back seat more comfortably than in some other brands up to 10 inches longer. We expect this Camry advantage to widen fractionally in this new model because both legroom and head­room in back are increased by a half-inch. Although the Camry is wider on the out­side, energy-absorbing padding to protect in side impacts takes up the extra space and, in certain spots, a little more. The Camry still has pockets in the front doors, unlike the Taurus, which sacrificed them for crash-protection equipment.

Those who wish to maximize rear-seat space should think twice about opting for power front seats (standard equipment on the top-of-the-line XLE). The manual­adjust buckets have excellent toeroom under them, which the power adjuster interrupts with a transverse bar. Tall folks won’t like that.

As in most modern sedans, the Camry has fold-forward rear seatbacks split one­-third and two-thirds, allowing the cargo compartment to be extended into the pas­senger area. Here’s another think-twice: Camrys equipped with the optional child seat—it’s built into the two-thirds section of the rear seat—have that section fixed in place, ruling out all but a narrow passage into the trunk.

At the rear, the trunklid opens wider and lower than before. Space inside, however, is a bit less in the new body—14.1 cubic feet versus 14.8 before. And the new car still has the conventional trunk hinges with the sickle arms that swing down into your luggage when the lid is closed.

Conventional is the right description for the new instrument panel, certainly more conventional than the old one, which tried to visually compartmentalize the cockpit by emphasizing a huge black field in front of the driver. That was the good part. The bad part was the deemphasized and totally boring padding it left for the passenger’s amusement. Now the all-new panel stretches its padding across the inte­rior in an equal-opportunity gesture that makes the interior seem brighter and wider. The glove box is 29 percent larger. The audio controls were raised to a mid­dash height, making them easy to see and reach. The climate controls have changed over to the increasingly common turn-to-adjust knobs. They’re large enough, and so obvious in their workings, that they are easy to operate in their less prominent location. The Camry continues to position its ignition switch in the dash where you can readily see it, instead of hiding it on the side of the steering column.

Toyota has proven itself to be the master of those little conveniences that add up to an exceptionally pleasing car. In this new Camry we see more clever trade-offs as the engineers cut costs, reduce weight, and usually end up serving the customer better, too. For example, the new front bumper cuts the part count nearly in half and saves weight, yet it increases protec­tion to 5 mph from 2.5. Inside, the seats recline in stepless increments now, and the buckets’ height adjusters use a single knob instead of two. Both of these changes cut costs, Toyota says. We say they make the car better, too. Models that previously would have had retracting antennas now have the antenna screened on the rear glass, saving weight and cost. The new Bosch anti-lock brake system weighs half as much as the old one.

Still, not every cost saver is a benefit. The LCD odometer is simply gray num­bers on a gray field, making it less visible than the glowing digits in competitors like the Chrysler Cirrus and the Dodge Stratus. And the new one-piece front-bumper cover now incorporates the grille into its overtly ordinary Rubbermaid-looking façade.

There’s been much speculation in the automotive-trade press about a possible price cut. Don’t hold your breath. Sales of the old Camry hit records earlier this year with no apparent price cutting. Were there sweeteners for the dealer? Sure, but other brands had them, too. Toyota knows all the tricks for selling cars without collapsing its price structure-tricks, we think, that mostly won’t be needed to move this shrewdly updated Camry.

#4316. NIO targets 10,000 battery swap stations and $52B in batteries by 2030

NIO says its energy arm, NIO Power, will operate more than 10,000 battery swap stations and manage over RMB 350 billion ($52 billion) worth of battery packs by 2030.

That’s more than double the swap network NIO runs in China today. And it comes from a company that already missed its last big swap station target.

NIO shared the targets today at NIO IN 2026, its annual technology event, held in Guangzhou to mark the company’s 12th anniversary. NIO Power also expects to deliver over 10 billion kWh of energy per year through charging and battery swapping by the end of the decade.

As of November 11, NIO had 4,252 battery swap stations in China, alongside 5,584 charging stations, according to the company’s latest network count.

Getting to 10,000 by 2030 means adding roughly 1,400 swap stations per year for four straight years. NIO added 679 in 2024 and 681 in 2025. So the new plan needs about double the company’s recent pace.

Even this year’s goal of “at least 1,000” new stations looks tight. NIO had 3,729 swap stations in February when it celebrated its 100 millionth swap, which means it has added just over 500 since then.

There’s also some history here. At its 2021 Power Day, NIO committed to more than 4,000 battery swap stations worldwide by the end of 2025, with about 1,000 of them outside China. By February 2026, it had about 3,700, almost all of them in China.

The energy target is just as aggressive. NIO’s swap network had delivered 5.28 billion kWh in total by February, after roughly eight years of operation. The 2030 goal is nearly twice that every year, although it also counts NIO’s charging stations.

NIO’s swap network is tied to its Battery-as-a-Service (BaaS) model, where customers can buy the car without the pack and rent the battery instead. That means someone has to own a massive fleet of packs, both in customers’ cars and sitting charged in stations. NIO says it wants to manage more than $52 billion of them in four years.

For context, NIO reported total revenue of about $4.7 billion in Q2 2026.

NIO has been moving the heavy capital off its own books. Under deals like its agreement with Zhongan Energy to build 500 swap stations within a year, partners own the stations while NIO handles the technology and operations. NIO Power says it has now co-built more than 900 swap stations with partners.

The hardware is also getting better. NIO opened its first fifth-generation swap stations in August, and they’re the first to serve all three of its brands. That includes the compact firefly, which couldn’t use older stations because of its shorter wheelbase.

NIO CFO Stanley Qu, who also heads NIO Power, presented the unit as NIO’s showcase for running a business with AI agents, using them to manage battery value, station operations, and energy efficiency.

The swap targets were only part of the event; everything else focused on NIO’s AI-fication.

NIO also launched NIO WorldModel (NWM) 3.0, the latest version of its driver-assist AI, which starts rolling out in December to vehicles with the Banyan, Cedar, Cedar S, and Coconut+ systems, pending regulatory clearance.

NIO says NWM 3.0 needs 40% fewer driver interventions than the previous version. It didn’t say how many interventions it started from, which makes the number hard to evaluate. It also claims a roughly 60% boost in drivers’ “sense of reassurance,” whatever that means.

The more concrete claims are about speed: NIO says overall vehicle control latency is down 54% and chassis control latency is down 78%, while training is five times more efficient.

NIO also unveiled NOMI Intelligence 4.0, a rebuild of its in-car assistant around an AI agent framework that can plan and carry out tasks on its own instead of following set commands. The first release, Cedar 2.0.0, will be filed in early December. Cars on Cedar S and Banyan should get it in Q2 2027, followed later by ONVO models.

Finally, CEO William Li pitched NIO as an “AI-native organization.” He argued the global auto industry is worth $7 to $9 trillion and that AI could add more than $1.2 trillion in value to it. NIO says it has deployed over 7,500 AI agents internally, with more than 2.9 million executions so far.

NIO’s swap network is real, and it works. The company passed 130 million swaps this month, and nobody else has built anything close at this scale. Tesla sort of tried battery swapping and quietly dropped it. NIO kept going.

BYD charges in 5 to 9 minutes. a swap takes 5 minutes. I don't know man. It doesn't look good for NIO.

But 10,000 stations by 2030 requires a build pace NIO has never hit, and its last swap target slipped badly. So we’d treat that number as an ambition, not a forecast.

The $52 billion battery figure is the interesting part. It shows what NIO Power really is: a battery asset manager that also builds stations. That only works if partners keep putting up the capital and the batteries keep earning money over their lifetime. NIO has been trying to get other automakers on board for years, with limited results – though it appears to be starting to attract more players.

And the competition isn’t standing still. Chinese automakers like BYD are pushing megawatt-level charging that adds hundreds of kilometers of range in about the time it takes to swap a battery. If ultra-fast charging becomes common, NIO’s swap advantage gets a lot thinner.

Battery swapping is one way to recharge in minutes, but if you drive an EV, charging at home on solar power is still the cheapest way to fuel it. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. #4315. Volkswagen’s new affordable electric SUV gets a sporty upgrade with GTI DNA

Volkswagen gave its entry-level electric SUV a sporty makeover with GTI-inspired performance. The new ID. Cross R-Line tops the range with added power and style, but there’s more to it than meets the eye.

The new Volkswagen ID. Cross R-Line is now available to order in Germany, starting at €37,225 (about $41,000), including VAT.

While VW’s R-Line is typically just a style and equipment upgrade rather than a true performance upgrade, the range-topping ID. Cross version borrows its electric motor, battery, and chassis from the ID. Polo GTI.

The flagship ID. Cross R-Line model, which will go on sale in March 2027, will use the same 222 hp (166 kW) front-mounted electric motor with up to 290 Nm of torque, which VW said enables it to sprint from 0 to 62 mph (0 to 100 km/h) in 6.9 seconds.

It will also use the same 52 kWh nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) battery, providing a WLTP range of up to 266 miles (428 km).

The range-topping version comes with VW’s custom chassis technology, also used in the ID. Polo GTI, which includes an electronically controlled front differential lock, DCC adaptive chassis control, and progressive steering.

As such, the flagship R-Line model is 15 mm lower than the standard ID. Cross. The lower ride height and front differential lock help to improve traction, driving stability, and control, while DCC automatically adjusts to road conditions.

The 222 hp (166 kW) version debuts with an exclusive new Traction profile with different drive modes, including Eco, Comfort, Sport, and Individual.

While pre-sales for the flagship version will open in March 2027, the entry-level ID. Cross R-Line is now available to order in Germany starting at €37,225 (about $41,000), including VAT.

The entry-level version uses a 132 hp (99 kW) electric motor and a 37 kWh battery, providing a WLTP range of up to 195 miles (314 km).

The entry-level version gains “extensive” R-Line standard equipment, including R-Line style bumpers, vertical daytime headlights, and 19″ alloy wheels.

Other standard features include Volkswagen’s interactive ID. Light with LED matrix headlights, Keyless Access, Adaptive Cruise Control (ACC), and a rear-view camera.

0 to 62 mph (0 to 100 km/h) in 6.9 seconds. Not very sporty : )

Inside, all ID. Cross R-Line models feature sports comfort seats, R-Line trim, and progressive steering as standard. It also gains the Innovision Pro infotainment package with the “IDA” voice assistant.

Volkswagen has yet to reveal prices for the flagship ID. Cross R-Line with the 222 hp (166 kW) and 52 kWh battery, but it will likely be closer to €40,000 ($44,000) when it goes on sale next March. Volkswagen’s ID. Polo GTI electric hot hatch starts at €39,995.

The new R-Line trim comes after Volkswagen opened orders for the standard entry-level ID. Cross last month, starting at €27,995 ($31,000).

What do you think of the new VW ID. Cross R-Line? Would you buy one in the US? Sadly, VW has no plans to bring the entry-level electric SUV to the US, but it will launch the ID. Tiguan in 2027, which will replace the ID.4 SUV.

#4312. Alzheimer’s breakthrough exposes a hidden flaw in the brain’s cleanup system

A gene that helps the brain contain harmful protein buildup may play a crucial role in Alzheimer's disease. Researchers at UVA Health have discovered that when this gene stops functioning properly, the brain's natural defenses become less effective, allowing toxic plaques to accumulate more rapidly. The findings could point toward new ways to detect, treat, or potentially prevent the disease.

The research, led by John Lukens, PhD, focused on a gene called CASS4, which previous studies had repeatedly linked to an increased risk of Alzheimer's. Until now, however, scientists knew little about what the gene actually does. The team discovered that CASS4 helps regulate microglia, specialized immune cells that act as the brain's cleanup and defense system. When the gene's activity was disrupted, these cells struggled to respond to harmful plaques. They also became much less effective at containing and compacting the toxic material, allowing the plaques to expand and spread more aggressively.

"These findings break new ground in our understanding of how this genetic risk factor contributes to Alzheimer's disease," said Lukens, director of UVA's Harrison Family Translational Research Center in Alzheimer's and Neurodegenerative Diseases. "Our work further suggests that defective CASS4 activity may serve as an early-onset biomarker to detect Alzheimer's and that therapeutic strategies which boost its function may offer a much-needed approach to treat this devastating brain disease."

How the Brain's Cleanup System Protects Against Alzheimer's

More than 6 million Americans are living with Alzheimer's, a progressive disease that gradually damages memory and thinking abilities. As the condition advances, people can lose the ability to recognize even their closest family members, including their own children. Alzheimer's is the sixth-leading cause of death in the United States, according to the figures cited by the researchers.

Two major changes in the brain are associated with the disease. One is the accumulation of amyloid-beta plaques, sticky deposits of protein that collect between nerve cells. The other is the formation of twisted tangles of a protein called tau. Both are hallmarks of Alzheimer's, but growing evidence suggests that the brain's immune system, particularly its microglia, also plays an important role in how the disease develops.

Microglia normally help protect the brain by responding to threats and managing harmful material. When amyloid-beta plaques appear, these immune cells can surround them with protective barriers and compress the deposits into smaller, more tightly packed structures. This containment process helps limit the damage the plaques can cause to surrounding brain tissue.

The UVA researchers found that CASS4 is important for maintaining this protective response. When the gene was disrupted in laboratory mice, microglia became less capable of controlling amyloid-beta plaques. As a result, the plaques accumulated more rapidly, nearby nerve cells called neurons suffered damage, and the animals experienced worsening cognitive function.

A Little-Known Alzheimer's Gene Reveals Its Role

"Despite CASS4 being an Alzheimer's risk gene, really nothing is known about what this gene does or how it affects the brain during disease. Our lab sought to address this major knowledge gap with this paper," said Addie Walsh, UVA physiology graduate student and first author of the paper. "These are important findings because they give us new insight into how this understudied AD risk gene functions in the brain and suggest that CASS4 may normally help microglia respond to amyloid pathology."

The researchers also discovered that losing CASS4 set off a series of changes in the activity of other genes. These widespread effects could have implications beyond Alzheimer's, potentially helping explain biological processes involved in other neurodegenerative diseases, which progressively damage nerve cells.

One of the most significant findings was where CASS4 appears to exert its influence. Scientists had previously suspected that the gene contributed to Alzheimer's primarily through its effects on neurons, the cells responsible for transmitting information throughout the brain. Instead, the new research indicates that its main role is in the immune system.

That distinction could be important for developing future treatments. Rather than focusing exclusively on neurons or the proteins that accumulate in Alzheimer's, researchers may be able to strengthen the immune cells that help protect the brain from those deposits. The UVA team believes that increasing CASS4 activity or improving microglial function could eventually offer ways to slow or prevent the disease.

A Potential New Target for Alzheimer's Treatments

"We are now actively exploring potential roles for CASS4 in multiple other neurodegenerative disorders and developing novel strategies to therapeutically target it," said Lukens, of the Department of Neuroscience at the University of Virginia School of Medicine. "Many in the field initially presumed that CASS4 was likely functioning in neurons to influence Alzheimer's. Our findings shift this paradigm by proving that CASS4 predominantly acts through the immune system. This is particularly exciting, as it has only been in recent years that immune-targeting strategies have been considered for the treatment of neurodegenerative diseases, and this remains an untapped therapeutic avenue with tremendous potential."

The findings suggest that the brain's immune defenses may offer an important opportunity for future Alzheimer's therapies. They also raise the possibility that defective CASS4 activity could eventually serve as an early warning sign of the disease, potentially helping doctors identify people at risk before more serious symptoms develop.

However, these possibilities remain to be tested. The experiments showing increased plaque buildup, neuronal damage, and cognitive decline were conducted in mice. Further research will be needed to determine whether targeting CASS4 can produce similar protective effects in humans.

The work is part of a broader effort at UVA to translate laboratory discoveries into treatments for serious diseases. Lukens leads the Harrison Family Translational Research Center in Alzheimer's and Neurodegenerative Diseases, which operates within UVA's newly established Paul and Diane Manning Institute of Biotechnology. The institute was created to accelerate the development of medicines and other therapies for complex medical conditions using advances from UVA's biomedical research programs.

Lukens is also a member of UVA's Center for Brain Immunology and Glia (BIG Center), which studies the roles of immune cells and other supporting cells in brain health and disease.

Walsh, meanwhile, is preparing to continue her research into the brain's immune system in a new position.

"I will be heading to Boston at the end of the year to start my postdoctoral research with the Neurodegeneration Team at the pharmaceutical company Novartis," she said. "I am looking forward to continuing to study microglia in neurodegeneration."

Alzheimer's Gene Discovery Published in Scientific Journal

The research was published in the Journal of Experimental Medicine. The authors are Adeline E. Walsh, Benjamin A. Davis, Joshua D. Samuels, William A. Mills III, Jessica M. Thanos, Alexis M. Johnson, Katelyn A. Moore, Michael A. Puchalski, Eric J. Steacy, Benjamin W. Wendell, Amélie Daugherty-Lopès, Adrian A. Shimpi, Ukpong B. Eyo and Lukens. The researchers reported having no financial interest in the work.

Among the contributors is Davis, a fourth-year biology student at UVA, who says participating in scientific research has helped shape his approach to problem-solving and his plans for a career in medicine.

"I think that undergraduate research develops a kind of critical thinking that is difficult to cultivate inside a classroom," he said. "My experience with research has taught me to approach questions systematically and never assume there will be a clear answer. As I prepare to apply to medical school, I know these experiences will shape how I approach clinical care and the broader field of science."

Funding came from the National Institutes of Health's National Institute on Aging through grants R01AG071996, R01AG087406, RF1AG078684 and R01AG086344. Additional support was provided by the Cure Alzheimer's Fund, the Owens Family Foundation, the Harrison Family Foundation, the Rick Sharp Foundation, and the Steven A. Newman AD Award.

#4311. EU pushes back Tesla ‘Full Self-Driving’ vote meeting again, now set for December 15

The EU committee that could approve Tesla’s “Full Self-Driving,” now sold in Europe as Tesla Assisted Driving, across the whole bloc won’t meet on December 1 as planned. The meeting is now December 15.

A European Commission spokesperson confirmed the new date to Reuters. The Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles (TCMV) has already discussed Tesla’s file at two meetings without putting it to a vote.

Two weeks isn’t much on its own. But it’s the latest in a long line of European dates that didn’t hold.

In late 2025, Tesla told owners the Dutch regulator RDW had “committed” to approving FSD in February 2026. The RDW publicly corrected it. The Dutch approval came on April 10. Tesla then pointed owners to an EU-wide vote on October 6, and the TCMV agenda for that meeting had no vote on it.

Even the new date took a minute to settle. Belgium’s Flanders transport ministry first said the meeting had moved to December 7 before the Commission clarified it’s December 15. Nobody has given a reason for the change.

And a meeting isn’t a vote. The committee can discuss the file again and push the decision into 2027. Elon Musk said on Tesla’s Q3 call in October that he’d be surprised if EU-wide approval took longer than the first quarter of 2027.

EU-wide approval needs at least 15 of the 27 member states, representing at least 65% of the EU’s population.

Twelve countries have recognized the Dutch approval so far: the Netherlands, Belgium, Croatia, Czechia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Latvia, Lithuania, Slovakia, Slovenia, and, last week, Italy, where Tesla has started the rollout. Using Eurostat population figures, we count those 12 at roughly 29% of the EU’s population.

Germany is the obvious next yes. Berlin got Tesla to drop the “Full Self-Driving” name in Europe and then cut the system’s speed margin from 50% to 10% over the limit in exchange for its support. That would bring the yes camp to about 47%.

So Tesla still needs France, or both Spain and Poland, to get over 65%. Not a sure thing. Sweden asked the EU in June to reject the system unless Tesla removed the ability to drive above the posted limit at all.

There’s also a catch for owners. According to Reuters, an EU-level rejection would invalidate the national approvals already granted. If the vote fails, drivers in Italy, the Netherlands, and the 10 other countries who are paying for the system today could lose it.

A two-week slip in a Brussels committee calendar isn’t too bad, but the delays are adding up. It’s December, the committee has other files, and nothing Reuters reported points to a problem specific to Tesla.

Article and headline should consistently refer to it as Tesla Assisted Driving as that is the name which Tesla has agreed to use in the EU. I think the other big question for EU approval is how easily can the driver avoid paying attention to the road.

We also don’t think most owners realize what’s at stake. If this vote goes the wrong way, the national approvals go with it. Italian owners who just got the system would lose it a few weeks later.

What would help Tesla’s case more than a new name and a lower speed cap is data. The RDW still hasn’t published its test results, and Tesla has never released disengagement data in Europe or anywhere else. Governments on the fence, like Sweden, want to see evidence the system is safe, not a rebrand.

December 15 is the next date to watch. Does Tesla walk into that room with Germany, France, or Spain on board, or does this slide into 2027?

#4310. Battlefield 6's latest update dubbed the game's simultaneously best and worst patch as it runs into all kinds of issues

What's likely going to be the last major Battlefield 6 update of the year has launched with a number of unexpected issues.

There’s been a lot of anticipation for Battlefield 6’s version 1.1.3.0 patch. The patch kicks off the third and final phase of the game’s first season, adding some new holiday-themed content. More the new content itself, the update’s biggest additions are almost entirely gameplay-related.

Unfortunately, for as much as the changes in 1.1.3.0 have been well received, the launch has been marred by a series of technical issues, some of which are a little unusual.

Immediately after patch 1.1.3.0 went live, players on PC started reporting massive stutters that would occur every few seconds. The issue is especially pronounced in Redsec Battle Royale, but much deadlier in traditional multiplayer.

Battlefield Studios quickly acknowledged it, pointing out a workaround that appears to be working for players on Steam. According to those players, going offline on Steam’s friends menu has fixed stuttering for them.

The issue remains for other players on PC, however, and the developer said it’s working on a proper fix.

Perhaps the most disrupting problem the patch has caused is one that prevents players from being able to interact with the game’s menu. Tiles become unresponsive, or outright unselectable when you try to hover near them.

Ironically, the top set of tiles designed to make it easy for players to quickly jump into the new content has been the most affected. Restarting the game sometimes fixes the issue, and some players report that it only happens upon first launch after installing the update.

But Battlefield Studios later clarified that, unsurprisingly, there’s an actual reason behind the bug. Once again, a fix is being investigated, and the developer will offer an update once some progress has been made.

A little further down the list of importance is an issue that stops players from being able to skip tiers within the new Winter Offensive bonus path in the game’s battle pass. BF Studios took out the feature entirely while it works on a fix, so while you can continue making progress in the bonus path, you won’t be able to skip tiers.

This is all a shame to see. Outside of all the problems, the meat of the new update has been almost universally praised. The visibility improvements, and netcode updates have been celebrated. Many players were also happy to see meaningful updates to footstep audio and overall clarity.

It’s also unusual for a Battlefield 6 patch to run into so many issues at launch. The sentiment around 1.1.3.0 so far is that it’s the game’s best and worst update yet. Hopefully those issues will be fixed before the development team breaks for the holidays.

Honda also appears to be switching to a column-mounted gear selector.

While Honda was once led by the Accord and Civic sedans, in today’s SUV-obsessed market, the CR-V has become the Japanese automaker’s most important model. Its biggest rival, the RAV4, was overhauled for 2026 and went hybrid only. Now, the CR-V will follow suit to stay competitive in the incredibly crowded compact SUV segment. Hybrid sales of the current-generation CR-V have been strong, accounting for over half of the SUV’s total sales so far this year, making it a perfect choice to launch Honda’s new platform and hybrid powertrain.

The CR-V will arrive on a new platform that Honda promises will be stiffer and lighter than before, taking a modular approach that will lead to greater parts sharing and reducing costs. This platform will presumably be adapted to underpin future versions of the Accord and Civic, along with Acura models such as the upcoming next-generation RDX Hybrid.

Honda will ditch the standard 190-hp 1.5-liter four-cylinder engine for the 2028 CR-V, which will arrive exclusively with the company’s new hybrid powertrain. The fifth generation of Honda’s two-motor hybrid setup will continue to use an Atkinson-cycle four-cylinder, along with a pair of electric motors, but the 2.0-liter engine will be a fresh design, featuring a new cooling system. As before, the electric motors will power the wheels most of the time, but the gas engine can also be engaged to directly drive the wheels.

See all results for new 2028 Honda CR-V Hybrid for sale near 90001

The electric motors are more compact than before, and Honda has developed a new battery too. The company says the new hybrid setup will bring improved power and efficiency, targeting 10 percent better fuel economy than the outgoing hybrid powertrain. The current CR-V Hybrid makes 205 horsepower and is rated at up to 38 mpg combined. We wouldn’t be surprised to see power increase to over 220 hp—the RAV4 makes 226 hp in FWD form and 236 hp with AWD—and fuel economy nudge up to just over 40 mpg.

The CR-V is expected to come with front-wheel drive standard and all-wheel drive optional, although it’s unclear if the latter will see the addition of a third electric motor. Honda will also likely include the S+ Shift feature seen on the Civic Hybrid and Prelude, which simulates a traditional transmission’s gearchanges and allows the driver to manually shift with the steering-wheel paddles.

The CR-V’s chief rival will continue to be the Toyota RAV4. However, the Hyundai Tucson Hybrid and Nissan Rogue Hybrid, which both enter a new generation for 2027, will also be strong competitors. The Jeep Cherokee, Kia Sportage Hybrid, and Subaru Forester Hybrid will be in the mix too, along with nonhybrid compact SUVs like the Volkswagen Tiguan.

The move to only offer a hybrid powertrain could see the CR-V’s entry price climb, which might alienate some buyers. Honda will also need to make sure it can match or exceed the efficiency of rivals like the RAV4 while still providing adequate performance and a spacious, usable cabin, given how closely matched the compact SUV space is these days. Moving away from physical interior controls could also upset the Honda faithful who are used to the company’s simple-to-use buttons.

Production is set to kick off at Honda’s factories in East Liberty, Ohio, and Greensburg, Indiana, in April 2027. Sales should begin shortly after, and with the current CR-V Hybrid starting at $37,580, we expect the next-generation model to come in at around $38,000.
